Smith, Group Theory pg.71 11 Abelian groups In this section we will discover the structure of all finite abelian groups. 11.1 Direct products Recall the definition of a direct product (Definition 2.1.3): If G and H are groups, then their direct product G × H is also a group, where G × H is the set {(g, h) ∣ g ∈ G, h ∈ H} with operation (g1, h1) ⋅ (g2, h2) = (g1g2, h1h2). This is usually referred to as the external direct product. External direct products are easy to work with, but hard to detect. We will now develop a technique for detecting direct products. Note that for finite groups, ∣G × H∣ = ∣G∣ ⋅ ∣H∣ because we have ∣G∣ choices for the first coordinate and ∣H∣ choices for the second. Proposition 11.1.1. Let G and H be groups. Then G × H ≅ H × G. Proof. You will prove this on a problem sheet. Lemma 11.1.2. Suppose M and N are normal subgroups of a group G, and M ∩ N = ⟨eG⟩. Then for all m ∈ M and all n ∈ N we have mn = nm. Proof. Note that n−1mn ∈ M (because M ⊴ G) and so n−1mnm −1 ∈ M . Also mnm−1 ∈ N (because N ⊴ G) and so n −1mnm −1 ∈ N . Hence n−1mnm −1 ∈ M ∩ N = ⟨eG⟩. Therefore n−1mnm −1 = eG and so mn = nm. Theorem 11.1.3. Suppose M and N are normal subgroups of a group G, and M ∩ N = ⟨eG⟩. Then M N ≤ G and M N ≅ M × N. Proof. By Lemma 4.2.4, we know that M N ≤ G. Every element in g ∈ M N can be written g = mn, for some m ∈ M and some n ∈ N . In fact, this way of writing g is unique, because if g = mn = m1n1 for some m1 ∈ M and n1 ∈ N then nn−1 1 = m −1m1. Hence both m−1m and nn−1 1 lie in M ∩ N = ⟨eG⟩. Therefore n = n1 and m = m1. Now define a function θ ∶ M N → M × N with θ(mn) = (m, n). By the above argument, θ is well-defined. • θ is a homomorphism: if m1, m2 ∈ M and n1, n2 ∈ N , then θ(m1n1)θ(m2n2) = (m1, n1)(m2, n2) = (m1m2, n1n2) = θ(m1m2n1n2), and by Lemma 11.1.2 we have that m1m2n1n2 = m1n1m2n2. • θ is one-to-one: if θ(m1n1) = θ(m2n2) then (m1, n1) = (m2, n2) and therefore m1 = m2 and n1 = n2. • θ is onto: any (m, n) ∈ M × N satisfies θ(mn) = (m, n). Remark 11.1.4. The converse to Theorem 11.1.3 is obviously true: the group M × N has normal subgroups ˆM = M ×⟨eN ⟩ and ˆN = ⟨eM ⟩×N and it is easy to check that ˆM ˆN = M ×N and ˆM ∩ ˆN = ⟨(eM , eN )⟩ = ⟨eM ×N ⟩. Definition 11.1.5. If G is a group with normal subgroups M and N such that M ∩ N = ⟨eG⟩ and G = M N , then G is said to be the internal direct product of M and N . What is the point?!. Internal and external direct products are essentially the same thing. They each have advantages: external direct products are easy to work with and internal direct products are easy to detect (just look for two normal subgroups whose intersection is trivial).
